report:
## Conclusion: The claim is well supported by strong clinical trial evidence

Abaloparatide does reduce vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and this claim is supported by high-quality randomized controlled trial data plus meta-analysis confirmation.

**Primary Evidence — ACTIVE Trial (JAMA, 2016):** This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 2,463 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, comparing 18 months of daily subcutaneous abaloparatide against placebo (and open-label teriparatide). The trial found abaloparatide reduced new vertebral fracture incidence by **86%** compared to placebo (new vertebral fracture rate ~0.58% vs. 4.2% with placebo), alongside a 43% reduction in nonvertebral fractures and 70% reduction in major osteoporotic fractures. This led directly to FDA approval (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640).

**Durability — ACTIVExtend follow-up:** When ACTIVE participants transitioned to open-label alendronate for an additional 24 months, fracture risk reductions were sustained through the full 43-month period, with an ~84% relative reduction in vertebral fractures maintained, including in high-risk subgroups by age and baseline risk (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jbmr.3848; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7515468/).

**Independent Confirmation — Network Meta-Analysis:** A meta-analysis published in Osteoporosis International pooling multiple trials confirmed abaloparatide significantly reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo and compares favorably to other osteoporosis treatments (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-019-04947-2).

**Bottom line:** This is one well-replicated, statistically robust finding from a large RCT, corroborated by extension studies and independent meta-analysis — strong evidence supporting the claim as true.
